claims.text: The starting alloy is nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11.
The starting alloy is prepared by standard powder metallurgy methods.
The starting alloy initially has a uniform distribution of Cr, Ta, W, and V.
The proposed intervention is vacuum annealing at 900–950 K for 30–60 minutes followed by rapid quenching.
The pre-anneal will produce modified grain-boundary complexions.
The pre-anneal drives selective solute partitioning that depletes Cr and V at grain boundaries.
Rapid quenching after annealing will retain the nanostructure.
Reducing grain-boundary Cr and V concentrations will limit the nucleation and growth of radiation-induced Cr/V precipitates.
Cr/V depletion effectively poisons radiation-induced precipitation nucleation sites.
The pre-anneal will preserve the nanostructure's irradiation-defect sink efficiency.
The proposed irradiation regime is 200 keV energetic-particle irradiation to approximately 8 dpa at 300–400 K.
At approximately 8 dpa, the treated alloy will have more than 50% lower radiation-induced Cr/V precipitate density than the unmodified alloy.
The treated alloy will retain negligible irradiation hardening.
The unmodified alloy exhibits radiation-induced precipitation under the specified irradiation conditions.
The unmodified alloy exhibits negligible irradiation hardening under the specified irradiation conditions.
The optimized pre-annealed microstructure will facilitate bulk consolidation and improve suitability for practical bulk fabrication.
Thermal exposures outside the stated processing and irradiation ranges may destabilize the complexions or reduce defect-sink efficiency.
The pre-anneal may cause unintended grain growth.
